hints.text: Look at the two terms separately. Each one is a perfect square, and they are joined by a minus sign. Which factoring pattern fits?
Use the difference of squares pattern $a^2 - b^2 = (a + b)(a - b)$ with $a = x$ and $b = 3$, because $9 = 3^2$.
The pattern gives $(x + 3)(x - 3)$, which is choice B.

learningObjective: Factor a difference of two squares.
explanation: Rewrite the expression as $x^2 - 3^2$, which shows that it is a difference of two squares.
The pattern $a^2 - b^2 = (a + b)(a - b)$ applies with $a = x$ and $b = 3$, giving $(x + 3)(x - 3)$.
Expanding confirms it, because the middle terms $-3x$ and $+3x$ cancel to leave $x^2 - 9$.
The equivalent expression is $(x + 3)(x - 3)$, which is choice B.

alternativeExplanations.title: Why the middle term vanishes
steps: That cancellation is the whole reason the difference of squares factors so cleanly.
It is the single most frequently used factoring pattern on the SAT — recognizing "square minus square" on sight is worth real points.
